sections.title: IPv4 Address Basics
sections.content:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four octets (0-255) in dotted-decimal, e.g. 192.168.1.10. It has a network portion and a host portion; the subnet mask (or CIDR prefix) says where the split is.
Classes (legacy, still tested):
Class | First octet | Default mask | Use
A | 1-126 | /8 (255.0.0.0) | Huge networks
B | 128-191 | /16 (255.255.0.0) | Medium
C | 192-223 | /24 (255.255.255.0) | Small
D | 224-239 | — | Multicast
E | 240-255 | — | Experimental
127.x.x.x is loopback (127.0.0.1 = localhost).
Private ranges (RFC 1918, not routable on the internet):
10.0.0.0/8  |  172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (/12)  |  192.168.0.0/16
APIPA: 169.254.0.0/16 — a host self-assigns here when DHCP fails (a troubleshooting clue: 'I have a 169.254 address' means no DHCP).
exam_tips: Memorize the three RFC1918 private ranges and APIPA (169.254.x.x = DHCP failed).
Class is set by the first octet: A 1-126, B 128-191, C 192-223.

sections.title: Subnet Masks & CIDR
sections.content:
The mask marks network bits (1s) and host bits (0s). CIDR notation counts the network bits: /24 = 255.255.255.0.
Key mask values per octet come from the host bits:
CIDR | Mask (last octet) | Block size | Usable hosts
/24 | 0 | 256 | 254
/25 | 128 | 128 | 126
/26 | 192 | 64 | 62
/27 | 224 | 32 | 30
/28 | 240 | 16 | 14
/29 | 248 | 8 | 6
/30 | 252 | 4 | 2
Formulas (h = number of host bits = 32 - prefix):
Total addresses in the block = 2^h.
Usable hosts = 2^h - 2 (subtract network address + broadcast address).
Number of subnets when borrowing b bits = 2^b.
The /30 (2 usable hosts) is the classic point-to-point link mask. A /31 (RFC 3021) is used for point-to-point links where the 2-host subtraction is waived.
exam_tips: Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2. The -2 is the network and broadcast addresses.
/30 is the standard mask for a router-to-router point-to-point link.

sections.title: How to Subnet — Step by Step
sections.content:
Goal: given an IP and prefix, find the network, broadcast, and host range.
Work in the 'interesting octet' — the one the mask splits.
1. Find the block size: 256 - (mask value in that octet). Example /26 -> mask 192 -> 256-192 = 64.
2. List the subnet boundaries by counting up by the block size: for 192.168.10.x /26 -> .0, .64, .128, .192.
3. Place your address in a block: 192.168.10.100 falls in the .64 block (64-127).
4. Network address = the start (192.168.10.64). Broadcast = next boundary minus 1 (192.168.10.127). Usable hosts = .65 to .126.
Second example: 172.16.0.0/20. Prefix 20 -> the third octet is interesting (mask 255.255.240.0). Block size = 256-240 = 16 in the third octet -> subnets 0, 16, 32... A host at 172.16.18.5 is in the 172.16.16.0 subnet (16-31), broadcast 172.16.31.255, hosts 172.16.16.1 - 172.16.31.254.
VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking): size each subnet to its need — allocate the largest subnets first, then carve smaller ones from what's left — to avoid wasting addresses.
exam_tips: Block size = 256 - the mask value in the interesting octet. This single trick solves most subnetting questions.
Network address = block start; broadcast = next block start minus 1.
VLSM: assign the largest subnet first to avoid overlaps and waste.

sections.title: IPv6 Essentials
sections.content:
IPv6 is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, e.g. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329. Shorten with two rules: drop leading zeros in a group, and replace ONE run of all-zero groups with '::' (only once). So that becomes 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.
Address types: global unicast (routable, like public IPv4), link-local (fe80::/10, auto-configured, stays on the local link), unique local (fc00::/7, private), and multicast (ff00::/8). IPv6 has NO broadcast.
SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets a host build its own address from the router advertisement — no DHCP server required (though DHCPv6 exists for extra options).
Dual stack (run IPv4 and IPv6 together) and tunneling (6to4, Teredo) are common migration methods.
Why IPv6: IPv4's ~4.3 billion addresses ran out; IPv6 provides a practically unlimited space and removes the need for NAT.
exam_tips: '::' can appear only once in an IPv6 address; it replaces the longest run of zero groups.
fe80::/10 = link-local (every IPv6 interface has one). IPv6 has no broadcast — it uses multicast.
SLAAC = host self-configures its IPv6 address from router advertisements.

concept_cards.hook: A 32-bit value marking which bits of an IP are network (1s) vs host (0s). /24 = 255.255.255.0.
256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet. Counting up by the block size gives the subnet boundaries — the core subnetting shortcut.
2^(number of host bits) - 2. The minus two accounts for the network address and the broadcast address.
Automatic Private IP Addressing (169.254.0.0/16) — a host self-assigns here when no DHCP server responds; a telltale sign of a DHCP failure.
Variable Length Subnet Masking — sizing each subnet to its host count (largest first) so address space isn't wasted.
Classless addressing that writes the mask as a bit count (/26) instead of dotted decimal, decoupling networks from the old A/B/C classes.
A double colon that replaces one run of consecutive all-zero 16-bit groups in an IPv6 address; it may be used only once per address.

practice_questions.q: A host has the IP 192.168.10.100/26. What is its network address?
practice_questions.explanation: A /26 has block size 64 (.0, .64, .128, .192). 100 falls in the .64 block, so the network is 192.168.10.64.

practice_questions.q: How many usable hosts are in a /29 subnet?
practice_questions.explanation: A /29 has 3 host bits: 2^3 - 2 = 6 usable addresses.

practice_questions.q: A workstation shows an address of 169.254.12.5. What does this indicate?
options: It is on the loopback interface
It failed to reach a DHCP server and self-assigned APIPA
It has a valid public IP
practice_questions.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA — assigned when DHCP fails, signaling a DHCP connectivity problem.

practice_questions.q: Which subnet mask is standard for a router-to-router point-to-point link with exactly two hosts?
practice_questions.explanation: A /30 provides exactly 2 usable addresses, ideal for a point-to-point link.

practice_questions.q: Which of these is a valid shortening of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329?
practice_questions.explanation: Drop leading zeros and replace one run of zero groups with '::' (used only once).

practice_questions.q: What is the broadcast address of the subnet containing 10.20.30.70/27?
practice_questions.explanation: A /27 has block size 32 (.64, .96). 70 is in the .64 block (64–95), so the broadcast is 10.20.30.95.

practice_questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /28 subnet provide?
practice_questions.explanation: A /28 has 4 host bits: 2^4 − 2 = 14 usable addresses.

practice_questions.q: You need at least 500 hosts in one subnet. What is the smallest prefix that works?
Which subnet does the address 172.16.140.10/22 belong to?
practice_questions.explanation: A /22 has block size 4 in the third octet (…136, 140, 144). 140 falls on a boundary, so the network is 172.16.140.0.

practice_questions.q: What subnet mask does a /19 correspond to?
